cards.front: What is Augmented Reality?
cards.back: AR **creates a connection between the physical world and digital information**, enhancing real-world experiences through overlays of digital data — integrating virtual elements into the user's environment. Examples given: **location-based services** and **barcode applications**.

cards.front: The 10 AR milestones, in order
cards.back: **1968** Sutherland *Sword of Damocles* (first HMD) · **1992** term coined by **Caudell & Mizell at Boeing** (aircraft wire assembly) · **1993** Feiner **KARMA** (maintenance) · **1994** UNC medical AR (fetal observation) · **1996** **Studierstube** (first collaborative) · **1997–2001** Japan's Mixed Reality Systems Lab · **1997** **Touring Machine** (first outdoor, GPS) · **1998** **ARQuake** (first outdoor game) · **2003** **Invisible Trains** (first handheld) · **2008** **Vuforia** (first practical smartphone tracking).

cards.front: The 7 AR application domains
cards.back: **Industry & Construction** · **Maintenance & Training** · **Medical** · **Navigation** · **Television & Entertainment** · **E-Commerce & Marketing** · **Gaming** (Pokémon GO, ARQuake). They map almost one-to-one onto the historical milestones.

cards.front: Scalar vs point vs vector
cards.back: **Scalar** — magnitude only (real/complex numbers). **Point** — position only; no magnitude or direction. **Vector** — magnitude and direction but **no position**.

cards.front: The four vector operations
cards.back: **Addition (head-to-tail rule)** → vector · **Scaling** (adjusts magnitude, preserves direction) → vector · **Dot product (inner)** — a **scalar** measuring similarity · **Cross product (outer)** — a **vector perpendicular** to both.

cards.front: Which point/vector operations are legal?
cards.back: vector+vector ✅ → vector · scalar×vector ✅ → vector · **point − point ✅ → vector** · **point + vector ✅ → point** · **point + point ❌ undefined**. The test: an operation is meaningful only if the answer **doesn't change when you move the origin**.

cards.front: Dot vs cross product — what each answers
cards.back: **Dot: 'how aligned are these?'** — max when parallel, **zero when perpendicular**. Gives diffuse lighting ($\mathbf n\cdot\mathbf l$) and backface culling. **Cross: 'what is perpendicular to both?'** — zero when parallel. Gives surface normals and rotation axes.

cards.front: The three-space hierarchy — what does each ADD?
cards.back: **Vector space**: scalars + vectors (direction & magnitude). **Affine space**: adds **POINTS** — plus vector-point addition and point-point subtraction; deliberately has **no privileged origin**. **Euclidean space**: adds **DISTANCE and SIZE** — lengths, angles.

cards.front: The three properties of a linear space
cards.back: **Closure** — sums and scalar products stay inside the space. **Associativity** — grouping (**brackets**) doesn't matter. **Commutativity** — **order** doesn't matter. (Matrix multiplication is associative but **not** commutative — which is why transformation *order* matters.)

cards.front: Why does graphics live in affine space?
cards.back: It needs **points** (vertices) and **vectors** (normals, directions) and the operations between them, but must **not depend on a privileged origin** — because object, world and camera frames each carry their own. Affine space is the smallest structure supporting all of that.

cards.front: What is a frame?
cards.back: **An origin $P_0$ plus three basis vectors $(\mathbf v_1,\mathbf v_2,\mathbf v_3)$.** A *coordinate system* is basis vectors alone — enough for **vectors**; a **point** additionally needs the origin. If asked what a frame consists of, the answer is **four things**.

cards.front: Representing a vector vs a point
cards.back: Vector: $\mathbf w = \alpha_1\mathbf v_1+\alpha_2\mathbf v_2+\alpha_3\mathbf v_3$ — no origin term. Point: $Q = \alpha_1\mathbf v_1+\alpha_2\mathbf v_2+\alpha_3\mathbf v_3 + P_0$. **The same vector has different representations in different bases** — the numbers are a description, not the geometry.

cards.front: Why must basis vectors be linearly independent?
cards.back: If they were dependent they would fail to **span** the space (a dimension is lost) and representations would not be **unique**. In graphics the basis is usually **orthonormal**, which additionally gives $\alpha_i = \mathbf w\cdot\mathbf v_i$ and makes the change-of-basis matrix orthogonal ($M^{-1}=M^{\mathsf T}$).

cards.front: The change-of-basis equation
cards.back: $\mathbf u = M\mathbf v$, where $M$ converts a representation from one basis to another; **$M^{-1}$ runs the conversion backwards**. $M$ is a **dictionary between two languages**, not an action — the geometry doesn't move, only the description.

cards.front: The three OpenGL frames and the model-view matrix
cards.back: **Model (object) frame** — local coordinates of an object. **World frame** — global positioning in the scene. **Camera (eye) frame** — relative to the viewpoint. OpenGL's **model-view matrix** fuses model→world→eye into one multiply, exploiting **associativity**.

cards.front: The two types of basis transformation
cards.back: **Translation of basis** — shifting the origin (a *point* operation). **Rotation of basis** — changing the orientation of the basis vectors (a *vector* operation). A general change of frame combines both, which is why one $4\times4$ matrix can capture it.

cards.front: What are homogeneous coordinates?
cards.back: A **4D representation for both points and vectors in 3D**, so that translation, scaling and rotation can all be applied by the **same kind of matrix multiplication**. A point $P(x,y,z)$ becomes a 4D column matrix over the basis $(\mathbf v_1,\mathbf v_2,\mathbf v_3,P_0)$.

cards.front: What does the fourth component $w$ mean?
cards.back: It is a **type tag**, not a coordinate. **$w=1$ → a point** (has location, translate me). **$w=0$ → a vector** (direction only, don't translate me). Applying a translation matrix to a $w=0$ column leaves it unchanged automatically — no special-casing.

cards.front: Why can't translation be a $3\times3$ matrix?
cards.back: Because translation is **not linear** — it doesn't fix the origin ($T(\mathbf 0)=\mathbf d\ne\mathbf 0$). In 3D you're stuck with $\mathbf p' = A\mathbf p + \mathbf d$ (a multiply **and** an add). In 4D it becomes an ordinary matrix multiply, so everything composes.

cards.front: The four benefits of homogeneous coordinates
cards.back: **Uniformity** — every affine transform is one $4\times4$ matrix. **Composability** — sequences become matrix products that can be precomputed. **Hardware** — GPUs implement $4\times4$ multiply as a primitive. **Projection** — perspective is a $4\times4$ matrix plus a divide by $w$.

cards.front: What does the homogeneous point $(x,y,z,w)$ with $w\ne0$ denote?
cards.back: The 3D point $(x/w,\ y/w,\ z/w)$ — so $(2,4,6,2)$ and $(1,2,3,1)$ are the **same point**. This **perspective divide** is dormant for affine transforms and is switched on by perspective projection. Points with $w=0$ are 'points at infinity' — i.e. pure directions.

cards.front: What is coordinate-free geometry?
cards.back: Geometry's essential relationships **do not depend on the arbitrary choice of origin and axes**. Coordinate systems provide context but are **arbitrary**; **distance, angle and orthogonality remain unchanged** across frames. The numbers are the description; the geometry is the thing.

cards.front: Why does an AR system need coordinate-free thinking?
cards.back: An AR headset has **no canonical origin** — the world frame is wherever the tracker initialised, and the camera frame moves constantly. Geometry that only worked in one frame would **break the moment the user turned their head**.

cards.front: The six OpenGL coordinate systems, in order
cards.back: **Object (Model) → World → Eye (Camera) → Clip → Normalized Device → Window (Screen).** Transformations: model matrix, view matrix, projection matrix, **perspective divide**, viewport transform.

cards.front: Where does the perspective divide happen?
cards.back: Between **Clip and NDC**. The projection matrix only *sets up* $w$; the hardware performs the $\div w$ afterwards, collapsing 4D homogeneous coordinates into the canonical $[-1,1]$ cube.

cards.front: Why does NDC exist as its own stage?
cards.back: It is **resolution-independent**: the same scene renders identically on a phone or a 4K display; **clipping** is done against a fixed canonical cube (much cheaper than an arbitrary frustum); and a headset can render **two viewports** (one per eye) by changing only the last step.

cards.front: World vs object coordinates
cards.back: **Object coordinates** are local to the model and define its **shape** (a car's origin at its centre). **World coordinates** are global and define **where that model sits** relative to a fixed world origin $(0,0,0)$. The **model transformation** converts one to the other.

cards.front: Why treat geometric objects as ADTs?
cards.back: So that **illegal geometry is unrepresentable**. If `point` and `vector` are distinct types, `p + q` is a **compile error** rather than a silently wrong number. It is the homogeneous $w$ tag expressed in the type system.

cards.front: The affine sum and its condition
cards.back: $P = \alpha_1 R + \alpha_2 Q$ is legal **iff $\alpha_1+\alpha_2 = 1$**. Proof: $= R + \alpha_2(Q-R)$ — point + (scalar × vector) = point, every step legal. It abbreviates *'start at $R$, travel a fraction $\alpha_2$ toward $Q$'*.

cards.front: Special cases of the affine sum
cards.back: $(1,0)\to R$ · $(0,1)\to Q$ · $(\frac12,\frac12)\to$ **midpoint** · both in $[0,1]\to$ a point **on the segment** (a **convex combination**) · one negative $\to$ on the **line** but outside the segment.

cards.front: What are barycentric coordinates and where are they used?
cards.back: The 3-point generalisation of the affine sum: $(\alpha_1,\alpha_2,\alpha_3)$ with $\sum\alpha_i=1$, addressing a location inside a triangle. **Every GPU uses them** — rasterisation interpolates colour, texture coordinates and depth across a triangle with exactly these weights.

cards.front: Convex object and convex hull
cards.back: **Convex object**: for any two points inside it, the **entire segment** joining them stays inside. **Convex hull**: the **smallest convex polygon completely enclosing** a set of points — the rubber band stretched around nails at every point.

cards.front: The seven convex hull algorithms
cards.back: **Gift-Wrapping (Jarvis March)** · **Quickhull** · **Divide and Conquer** · **Monotone Chain** · **Incremental** · **Chan's Algorithm** · **Graham's Scan**. Complexities: Jarvis $O(nh)$, Graham $O(n\log n)$, Chan $O(n\log h)$ (optimal).

cards.front: Graham's scan in four steps
cards.back: 1. **Anchor** — pick $p_0$, the lowermost point (leftmost on a tie); it's guaranteed on the hull. 2. **Sort** the rest by **polar angle** about $p_0$. 3. **Scan** with a stack: **left turn → push**, **non-left turn → pop** (repeat, since removing one dent exposes another). 4. The stack is the hull.

cards.front: How is the turn test computed in Graham's scan?
cards.back: By the **sign of the cross product**, not an angle: for $A,B,C$, the scalar $(B_x{-}A_x)(C_y{-}B_y)-(B_y{-}A_y)(C_x{-}B_x)$ — positive = left, negative = right, zero = collinear. **Collinear counts as non-left and is popped**, removing redundant vertices along a straight edge.

cards.front: Applications of the convex hull
cards.back: **Geometry · robotic path planning · computer graphics · collision detection · shadows and lighting calculations.** In AR/VR: exact mesh-vs-mesh collision is too slow at 90 fps, so engines test **hulls first** — if the hulls miss, the meshes certainly do.

cards.front: What is a transformation, formally?
cards.back: A function mapping a point or vector to another: **$Q = T(P)$** for points, **$\mathbf v = R(\mathbf u)$** for vectors. The **linearity constraint** preserves linear combinations — i.e. **straight lines stay straight and midpoints stay midpoints**, which is why you can transform only the vertices of a mesh.

cards.front: Degrees of freedom: vectors vs points
cards.back: **Vectors: 9** (a $3\times3$ linear map). **Points: 12** (9 + a 3-vector translation). These are the 12 free entries in the top three rows of the $4\times4$ homogeneous matrix; the bottom row is fixed at $[0\ 0\ 0\ 1]$ — the moment it isn't, the map is a **projection**, not affine.

cards.front: Rigid vs non-rigid body transformations
cards.back: **Rigid** = rotation + translation: **preserve shape and volume**, affect only location and orientation, and **cannot achieve all affine transformations**. **Non-rigid** = scaling + reflection: change size and/or handedness.

cards.front: The scaling factor $\beta$ — three regimes
cards.back: **$\beta>1$** expands · **$0<\beta<1$** shrinks · **$\beta<0$ reflects**. Scaling has **6 DOF** (fixed point + 3 scale factors), dropping to 3 if the fixed point is the origin. A negative scale **flips handedness**, reversing triangle winding — the usual cause of an inside-out mirrored model.

cards.front: The translation matrix
cards.back: $T(\mathbf d)$ = identity with $(d_x,d_y,d_z)$ in the fourth column; $T^{-1} = T(-\mathbf d)$. Applied to a $w=0$ column it does **nothing** — directions are correctly left untranslated.

cards.front: Why are rotation matrices orthogonal, and why does it matter?
cards.back: A rotation maps an orthonormal basis to an orthonormal basis, so $R$'s columns are mutually perpendicular unit vectors → $R\,R^{\mathsf T}=I$, i.e. **$R^{-1}=R^{\mathsf T}$**. Undoing a rotation is therefore **free**. Also $\det R = +1$, so rotations never flip handedness.

cards.front: The sign-pattern trap in rotation matrices
cards.back: **$R_y$ has its minus sign in the bottom-left**, opposite to $R_x$ and $R_z$ — because rotation about $y$ carries $+z$ toward $+x$. Sanity check: **the axis of rotation always appears as a row and column of the identity** ($R_x$ → first, $R_y$ → second, $R_z$ → third).

cards.front: Transformation about an arbitrary fixed point — the pattern
cards.back: The **sandwich**: $T(F)\,S(\beta)\,T(-F)$ — translate the fixed point to the origin, do the simple thing, translate back. Read **right to left**. The same pattern handles rotation about an arbitrary point or axis.

cards.front: What does shear preserve, and what does it destroy?
cards.back: Preserves **straight lines, parallelism, ratios along a line** (and area/volume for a simple shear). **Destroys angles.** Shear is why 'affine' is strictly larger than 'rigid + scale' — you cannot build one from rotations and axis scalings.

cards.front: Concatenation: $q=CBAp$ vs $M=CBA$
cards.back: Both give the same answer (**associativity**), but differ in cost. **One point** → $C(B(Ap))$: three cheap matrix-vector products. **Many points** → build $M=CBA$ once (two expensive matrix-matrix products), then one cheap product per point. This is why OpenGL keeps a single model-view matrix.

cards.front: Order of transformations — the rule
cards.back: Matrix multiplication is **associative but NOT commutative**. Read $q = CBAp$ **right to left**: $A$ first. With column vectors the **first-applied transformation is rightmost**. Rotate-then-translate ≠ translate-then-rotate.

cards.front: Rotation about an arbitrary axis — the five steps
cards.back: 1. **$T$** — translate a point on the axis to the origin. 2. **$R_x$** — bring the axis into the $xz$-plane. 3. **$R_y$** — align the axis with $z$. 4. **$R_z(\theta)$** — do the actual rotation. 5. **Undo 3, 2, 1** in reverse. Principle: *you only know how to rotate about $x,y,z$ — move the problem until it is one of those.*

cards.front: Inverting a composite transformation
cards.back: **$(CBA)^{-1} = A^{-1}B^{-1}C^{-1}$** — invert each factor **and reverse the order**. For rotations each inverse is just a **transpose**.

cards.front: How to sanity-check a composite matrix
cards.back: **Bottom row** must still be $[0\ 0\ 0\ 1]$ (it's affine). **Translation column** should match the last-applied translation. **Determinant** of the upper-left $3\times3$: rotations contribute 1, a uniform scale by $\beta$ contributes $\beta^3$, a reflection makes it negative.

cards.front: Why do complex numbers lead to quaternions?
cards.back: **Multiplying by a unit complex number rotates the plane**, and multiplying two of them **adds their angles** ($e^{i\theta}=\cos\theta+i\sin\theta$). Quaternions are the answer to *'what is the 3D version of that trick?'*

cards.front: The quaternion form and the Hamilton relations
cards.back: $H = a+bi+cj+dk$ — one **real (scalar)** part and three **imaginary (vector)** parts. **$i^2=j^2=k^2=ijk=-1$**, with $ij=k,\ jk=i,\ ki=j$ (and $ji=-k$ etc.). ⚠ The course booklet misprints the squares as **0** — that is wrong.

cards.front: Why is quaternion multiplication non-commutative?
cards.back: Because **3D rotations don't commute** — turning right then looking up ≠ looking up then turning right. $ij=k$ but $ji=-k$. An algebra that *did* commute could not model 3D rotation.

cards.front: What is gimbal lock?
cards.back: With Euler angles, when the **middle rotation reaches ±90°** the first and third axes align and a **degree of freedom is lost** — no combination of the three angles can produce rotation in the lost direction. It's a **topological** property of using only three numbers; the escape is a fourth, i.e. quaternions.

cards.front: Euler vs matrix vs quaternion
cards.back: **Euler**: 3 numbers, **gimbal lock**, poor interpolation. **Matrix**: 9 numbers, no lock, interpolates badly (needs re-orthonormalisation), 27 multiplies to compose. **Quaternion**: **4 numbers, no lock, slerp interpolation, 16 multiplies**.

cards.front: Component-order trap
cards.back: This course uses **both** $(w,x,y,z)$ and $(x,y,z,w)$. Always read the stem. Tell: for small rotations $w=\cos(\theta/2)$ is **close to 1**, so the component nearest 1 is usually the scalar.

cards.front: Axis-angle → quaternion, and back
cards.back: **Forward:** $q = (\cos\frac{\theta}{2},\ \hat{\mathbf u}\sin\frac{\theta}{2})$. **Backward:** $\theta = 2\arccos(w)$, $\hat{\mathbf u} = (x,y,z)/\sin(\theta/2)$. **The half-angle is the #1 mistake in this unit.**

cards.front: Why the half-angle?
cards.back: Because the rotation formula applies $q$ **twice** — once on each side of the sandwich product $\mathbf v' = q\,\mathbf v\,q^{-1}$ — so each application contributes half the rotation. It is also the root of the **double-cover** property.

cards.front: How is a vector rotated by a quaternion?
cards.back: Embed it as a **pure quaternion** $(0,\mathbf v)$ and form the **sandwich product** $\mathbf v' = q\,\mathbf v\,q^{-1}$. For a unit quaternion $q^{-1} = \bar q = (w,-x,-y,-z)$ — the **conjugate**.

cards.front: Composing rotations and finding the rotation between two orientations
cards.back: Applying $q_1$ then $q_2$ gives **$q_2q_1$** (right-to-left, like matrices). The rotation carrying orientation $q_1$ to $q_2$ is **$\Delta q = q_2\,q_1^{-1}$**.

cards.front: Single cover vs double cover
cards.back: **Rotation matrices are single cover** — one matrix per rotation. **Quaternions are double cover** — **$q$ and $-q$ represent the same rotation**, because the two minus signs cancel in $q\mathbf vq^{-1}$. It's the half-angle's shadow: $\theta$ and $\theta+360°$ differ by $180°$ in the half-angle, flipping every sign.

cards.front: Why does the sign of a quaternion matter for slerp?
cards.back: The **orientation** is identical for $q$ and $-q$, but **interpolating** between opposite-signed quaternions takes the **long way round** (a 350° swing instead of 10°). Real slerp implementations check $q_1\cdot q_2<0$ and negate one first — otherwise objects snap almost the whole way around.

cards.front: The Hamilton product formula
The four checks for any quaternion problem
cards.back: 1. Is it **unit length** ($w^2+x^2+y^2+z^2=1$)? 2. **Which component is $w$** — check the stated ordering. 3. Did you **halve** the angle going in and **double** it coming out? 4. Does **$w$ near 1** correspond to a **small** rotation in your answer?

cards.front: What is slerp and why does it beat matrix interpolation?
cards.back: **Spherical linear interpolation** — unit quaternions live on a 4D unit sphere, so interpolating along that surface gives **constant angular velocity** and visibly smooth rotation. Linearly interpolating rotation matrices leaves intermediates **non-orthogonal** (they squash the object) and needs re-orthonormalisation each step.
